idiom_name: closure over receiver and parameters; { execute, undo } object when the inverse must travel with the request
implementation_notes: JavaScript needs no ConcreteCommand class: MDN's closure guide states the practical equivalence directly - a closure associates data with a function, so it can be used anywhere an object with a single method would be used. Commands are therefore plain functions in a queue or history array, Function.prototype.bind supplies the receiver when a method has to be detached from its object, and undo is either a second closure stored next to the forward one or a small object exposing execute/undo. The class form earns its keep only when requests must be identified, persisted or extended polymorphically.
pitfalls: A method passed as a command loses its receiver (this becomes undefined in modules or strict mode); bind it or wrap it in an arrow function, exactly as MDN documents for callbacks.
Closures capture variables, not values, so a command built in a loop over a mutated variable or a shared object applies the later state when the invoker eventually runs it.
Nothing enforces the execute/undo contract at run time - a typo or a forgotten inverse only fails when the history is used, so funnel command creation through one factory.
A long-lived history keeps every captured receiver reachable, which in DOM code leaks detached nodes and their listeners.
